questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩=⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2c\operatorname{cos}⁡x-cy=8 \\ -xc=2\pi  \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-x(-2)=2\pi \,⟹\,x=\pi .
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $x=\pi $ into the first equation, we have 

$$
2(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-2)y=8\,⟹\,y=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\pi $ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -(\pi )(2) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(\pi ,2,-2\pi ).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2})$ at the point $(1,-1,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=-\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)-2(y+1)-2(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2-2y-2-2z+2 \\ -2x+2y+2z+w+2 & =0 \\ 2x-2y-2z-w-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ at the point $(1,1,\pi ,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi )+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi )+(z-\pi )\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi (x-1)-\pi (y-1)-(z-\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi x+\pi -\pi y+\pi -z+\pi  \\ \pi x+\pi y+z+w-3\pi  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y+6=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$
z={1}^{2}-2(1)+(-3)^{2}+6(-3)+10=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$

questions.problem: At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6cx=4 \\ 2cy=-2 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$
